papers.title: Supporting a Mindful, Reflective, Caring Practice in Nursing Capstone Students.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: How do you engage students in substantive reflection in an asynchronous online course? This article proposes a shift from resilience toward sustained, supported reflective practice that supports nurse agency. METHOD: Rather than teach reflection, students are introduced to models that support the development and practice of mindful intention and reflective practice that emphasizes strengths and appreciation. Students are provided with tools to promote reflection, creativity, affective learning, and diversity, equity, and inclusion. Students engage in forums, journals, and ePortfolio platforms, transforming an asynchronous online course into a nontraditional community of practice. RESULTS: The integration of Caring Arts into a Nursing capstone course supported the development and practice of mindful intention, reflection, independent thought, and the actualization of evidence-based practice. CONCLUSION: In a senior capstone course, nursing students experienced guided reflective practice supported by visual thinking strategies, nonviolent communication

papers.title: Overcoming essentialism: evaluation of theories of consciousness by the lawful regularities they predict.
papers.abstract: A common objection to consciousness research is that researchers cannot agree on what consciousness is. But how should a consensus on the nature of consciousness be reached? Does consciousness have essential features that one can be right or wrong about? Should we select theories of consciousness based on their descriptions of the essential features of experience alone? In this article, we will argue with the help of Popper that determining unquestionable essential features of consciousness is neither possible nor desirable. Instead, any account of what consciousness is, should be understood as a subjective selection of features and should not count as an insight. According to Popper, insights in science are achieved when novel regularities between observations are discovered that generalize to scientific laws. Furthermore, all results of research can be stated independently of the definitions that were used in their making. Therefore, no consensus on the nature of consciousness or on a theory of consciousness is needed for consciousness research to progress-in fact, a multitude of definitions and theories may be beneficial. Based on this, we argue that theories of consciousness be evaluated by their ability to propose concrete, testable laws rather than by their description of what consciousness is.

papers.title: Longer term impact of universal school-based mindfulness training compared with normal school provision on adolescent mental health and well-being, teacher mental health and school climate: results from the 2-year follow-up in the MYRIAD cluster randomised controlled trial.
Mapping three decades of consciousness research in neuroscience: a scientometric synthesis of intellectual evolution and emerging frontiers.
papers.abstract: Over the past three decades, consciousness research in neuroscience has expanded into a broad and increasingly diverse field. Despite significant progress, a quantitative understanding of how these research areas have collectively evolved has remained limited. In this study, we conducted a large-scale scientometric analysis of consciousness research in neuroscience based on 22,836 publications and 639,975 cited references retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection spanning 1998-2025. We identified three major research paths: neural correlates of conscious contents and states, internal awareness and self-consciousness, and integrative approaches bridging these two paths. Emerging hotspots included neural mechanisms of consciousness, subjective experience, disorders of consciousness (DoC), and interoception. Despite increasing boundary-spanning research across different areas, bibliometric connections between DoC and other major topics, particularly subjective experience and interoception, remain comparatively sparse. These findings provide a field-level synthesis of consciousness research in neuroscience, offering a quantitative framework for understanding its development and emerging research directions.
